en: Compiled by the National Preceptor of the Chen and Sui Dynasties, the Great Master Zhizhe.
Chapter One: The Initial Gate of Name-and-Form (Nāmarūpa). Section One:
Name (Nāman). Section Two: Form (Rūpa).
Now, in distinguishing the initial gateway to the Dharma-realm,
we first begin from name-and-form;
this leads to the treatise on the fundamental purity of all phenomena.
Transcending names and detached from marks, it is not even one;
how could there ever have been two?
To distinguish these two while they are non-dual:
when a practitioner first receives the deluded retribution of a single lifetime at the stage of the *kalala*,
there are only the two dharmas of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
One should know that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the very root of all mundane and supramundane phenomena;
it is able to give rise to all phenomena and universally encompasses all phenomena.
This refers to all phenomena.
Whenever the Great Sages provide analytical explanations of the various gateways to all phenomena,
they do so by analyzing them in terms of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
There is not a single dharma that exists apart from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Thus, a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Among all dharmas, there are only name and form."
If one wishes to contemplate according to reality, one should contemplate only name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Although the deluded mind conceives many thoughts and discriminates various phenomena,
there is not a single dharma that exists apart from name-and-form.
First is "name" (*nāman*): because the mind possesses only words, it is called a "name.
This refers to the mind and its associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
Although they possess the function of being cognitive objects, they lack any material obstruction that can be perceived.

Since these differ from form (*rūpa*) and possess various distinct designations such as mind (*citta*), mental consciousness (*manas*), and the various numerical factors (*dharmāḥ*), they are called "name" (*nāma*).
Second, form: phenomena that possess physical shape and resistance are called "form."
These ten bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base are all material phenomena characterized by resistance;
they possess no faculty of cognition.
Since it differs from the dharmas of mind, intellect, and consciousness, it is termed "form" (*rūpa*).

Second, the initial gateway of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*): first, the aggregate of form; second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā*); third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā*); fourth, the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra*); fifth, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Following the explanation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the five aggregates are now distinguished.
Because those who are deluded are confused by names and place undue emphasis on them,
the Great Sage’s gateway of teaching opens up names into four mental states;
when combined with form, they constitute the five aggregates.
Regarding why these five are called "aggregates" (skandha):
to explain briefly,
"aggregate" has the meaning of "covering" or "heaping up."
It can obscure the wisdom of supramundane, true illumination,
thereby increasing birth and death so that their accumulation and dispersal continue without end.
Therefore, they are collectively termed "aggregates" (*skandha*).
First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*): phenomena that possess physical substance and resistance are called "form.
There are fourteen kinds of form.
That which is called the four great elements, the five faculties, and the five objects—
these fourteen are all material phenomena (rūpadharma).
2. The Aggregate of Feeling (vedanā-skandha). That which experiences the object is called feeling.
There are six kinds of feeling;
that is to say, six feelings arise conditioned by the six types of contact.
Since objects of perception already possess the distinctions of being disagreeable,
agreeable, or neither disagreeable nor agreeable,
the six types of feeling likewise each have their own painful feelings and pleasant feelings.
This is the distinction between feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant.
Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): the grasping of the characteristics of objects that are experienced is called perception.
There are six kinds of perception.
That is to say, grasping the characteristics of the six objects of perception that are experienced constitutes the six types of perception (*saṃjñā*).
Regarding the four aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): the mind that performs volitional activity and is capable of tending toward a result is called formations.
There are six kinds of formations (*saṃskāra*);
in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*,
they are explained as the six volitions (*cetanā*).
Volition is precisely action;
that is to say, following each of the six types of perception,
there arise respectively unwholesome karma, wholesome karma, and immovable karma.
The five aggregates of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*): that which discerns the objects of perception is called consciousness.
There are six kinds of consciousness;
these are the six consciousnesses.
If various masters of the treatises mostly say that consciousness exists prior to the two minds,
[as stated] in the Mahāyāna sūtras:
Clear consciousness is placed last. Now, following the Sūtra, we shall analyze them in their proper order. **Chapter Three:

The Initial Gate of the Twelve Bases (Āyatana)** The Six Internal Sense-Bases (Indriya-āyatana): 1. The eye-base 2. The ear-base 3. The nose-base 4. The tongue-base 5. The body-base 6. The mind-base The Six External Sense-Objects (Viṣaya-āyatana): 1. The form-base 2. The sound-base 3. The odor-base 4. The taste-base 5. The tangible-base 6. The mental-object-base Regarding the analysis of the twelve bases following the five aggregates (skandha): [the text continues as follows: ...the reason for distinguishing the twelve bases after the five aggregates is that... [text continues].
Because those who are deluded are biased toward and attached to form,
the Great Sage’s teaching opens up form into ten categories.
The mind consists of only two;
together they constitute the twelve.
They are collectively termed "entrances" (āyatana).
"Entering" (āyatana) takes the sense of "penetrating into.
When the faculties and their objects encounter one another, consciousness arises;
since consciousness relies upon the faculties and objects, it remains that which enters.
The faculties (indriya) and objects (viṣaya) are precisely that which is entered.
Now, these twelve [bases] receive their name from that which is entered;
therefore, they collectively receive the name "entrances" (āyatana).
Regarding the six internal bases:
these six factors are classified as internal because they are proximate;
they serve as the supports for consciousness.
Therefore, it is called "entry" (praveśa).
It is also called a "faculty" (indriya);
"faculty" has the meaning of being able to produce [something].
Since these six all possess the function of producing consciousness, they are collectively termed "faculties" (indriya).
First is the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana):
it is a part of the body that confronts visible forms.
The locus capable of seeing forms is called the eye.
The eye is composed of the four great elements and derived matter;
its substance is formed by the ten types of material phenomena.
These are the so-called four great elements and the four subtle particles:
the subtle particle of the body faculty and the subtle particle of the eye faculty.
Second, the ear-base (*śrotra-āyatana*): that part of the body which faces sound and is capable of hearing sound is called the "ear.
The ear is derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*) composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
It is also composed of ten substances: namely,
the four great elements (mahābhūta), the four subtle elements (tanmātra), and the subtle element of the body faculty (kāyendriya-tanmātra).
The faculty of the ear is subtle.
Third, the nose-base: the portion of the body that encounters fragrance and is capable of smelling it is called the nose.
The nose is composed of the four great elements and derived matter;
it is also constituted by ten types of matter,
namely, the four great elements and the four subtle particles.
The body faculty is subtle;
the nose faculty is subtle.
Regarding the four tongue bases: the body part encounters flavors.
That which is capable of knowing tastes is called the tongue.
The tongue is composed of the four great elements and is also formed by the ten types of derived matter.
That is to say, the four great elements and the four subtle elements:
the subtle element of the body faculty and the subtle element of the tongue faculty.
The five bodies and six parts constitute a body that is a provisional combination;
that which can perceive contact wherever it occurs is called the body.
The body is matter derived from the four great elements.
It consists solely of nine material elements:
namely, the four great elements, the four subtle elements,
and the subtle element of the body faculty.
There are six mental sense-bases (*manāyatana*). When the mind encounters all phenomena (*dharma*),
it possesses the functional capacity to cognize those phenomena.
It is named "mind" (*manas*).
"Mind" refers to the sovereign mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
Within this, all mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*) are excluded.
One takes only the mind-king (citta-rāja) as the internal sense-base (āyatana);
as for the six external sense-bases (bāhyāyatana):
Because these six factors are coarse, they are categorized as external;
because consciousness traverses and engages with them,
they are called "entrances" (āyatana).
They are also called "objects" (*rajas*).
"Object" has the meaning of defilement,
as they are able to defile the sensory consciousnesses.
Therefore, they are collectively termed "objects" (*viṣaya*).
First, the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*):
all that is perceived by the eye is called "form."
Form consists of two kinds of form that encompass all forms:
first, visible form as the primary retribution (*vipāka*).
The physical forms and colors of sentient beings—
such as blue, yellow, red, white, and black—
as well as the second type, the visible forms of the environment they rely upon.
Externally, there is no cognition of blue, yellow, red, white, or black colors and so forth.
Second, the sphere of sound (*śabda-āyatana*): All that is encountered by the ear is what is called "sound" among the objects perceived.
There are two kinds of sound that encompass all sounds: first,
sound produced from the matter of the primary retribution (vipākaja-rūpa).
First, it is the sounds and voices of sentient beings.
Second, it is the sound emerging from the matter of the external environment.
Third, regarding the sense-base of fragrance: all [fragrances] encounter the nose.
Regarding the forms, names, and fragrances that are heard:
fragrance is of two kinds,
which encompass all fragrances.
First, the fragrance of the sense-object of form as primary retribution (*vipāka*),
which refers to the fragrances and odors within the bodies of sentient beings.
Second, the fragrance of the sense-object of form as secondary retribution (*adhipatiphala*).
All odors and smells contained within all external insentient forms are the four taste-entrances (*rasāyatana*).
All forms known by the tongue are called taste (*rasa*).
Taste has two kinds of taste that encompass all tastes:
first, the taste of the objective field of form as primary retribution (*vipāka*).
These are the six flavors within the bodies of sentient beings.
Second is the flavor of the objective environment (*upādāya-rūpa*): the six flavors present within all external, insentient forms.
The five spheres of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*):
all that is perceived by the body is called tangibility.
There are two kinds of tangibility.
It encompasses all types of contact (*spraṣṭavya*).
First, there is the contact of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) as the primary retribution within the bodies of sentient beings.
The sixteen tangibles, such as cold, heat, roughness, smoothness, and so forth.

Second, the tangibles of the objective sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) based on external conditions: these are the sixteen tangibles, such as cold, heat, and so forth, among all external insentient forms.
The Sixfold Entrance into Phenomena: All phenomena that are objects of mental cognition are called "phenomena" (*dharma*).
There are two kinds of phenomena that encompass all phenomena.
The first is mental phenomena (*caitasika-dharma*).
Within this category, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is excluded;
only the various associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are included.
The second category consists of non-mental phenomena (*acaitasika-dharma*),
namely: past and future form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and all formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

And the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). **The First Gate of the Eighteen Elements (18 Dhātus), Part Four: The Six Internal Sense-Bases (Āyatana) Elements** 1. Eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*) 2. Ear element (*śrotradhātu*) 3. Nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) 4. Tongue element (*jihvādhātu*) 5. Body element (*kāyadhātu*) 6. Mind element (*manodhātu*) **The Six External Sense-Object Elements** 1. Form element (*rūpadhātu*) 2. Sound element (*śabdadhātu*) 3. Odor element (*gandhadhātu*) 4. Taste element (*rasadhātu*) 5. Tangible object element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) 6. Mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*) **The Six Consciousness Elements** 1. Eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) 2. Ear-consciousness element (*śrotravijñānadhātu*) 3. Nose-consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*) 4. Tongue-consciousness element (*jihvāvijñānadhātu*) 5. Body-consciousness element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*) 6. Mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) Next, the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
As for the differentiation of the eighteen *dhātus*,
it is because those who are deluded are confused by the fact that both name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*) are equally substantial;
therefore, form is divided into ten.
When distinguished, they are called eight;
when combined, they constitute the eighteen *dhātus*.
As for their common designation as "elements" (*dhātu*):
They are defined by way of their distinct elements (*dhātu*);
these eighteen phenomena each possess a distinct substantial entity,
so that their meanings are neither confused nor conflated.
Therefore, they are collectively designated by the name "dhātu.
Regarding the six internal sense-bases (āyatana) of the faculties, these are fully explained as previously stated;
their specific characteristics are analyzed within the context of the six internal sense-bases.
Furthermore, the reason for adding the terminology of "realms" (dhātu) is to enable practitioners of meditation to analyze [phenomena] without error,
so that they do not become stuck in the false conceptualizations of the sixteen views.
Regarding the six external spheres of objects (*viṣaya-dhātu*): these are as previously detailed.
Within the six external bases of consciousness (*āyatana*), their characteristics are further analyzed by adding the designation and meaning of "sphere" (*dhātu*).
The mental faculty (manas) is treated similarly to the six sense organs;
thus, the term "element" (dhātu) is established for it.
As for the six consciousness elements (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātavaḥ):
If the sense faculty and its object encounter one another, consciousness arises.
The defining characteristic of consciousness is discernment;
consciousness depends upon the sense faculty.
Because they are able to discern objects,
these six are called consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
If one understands that consciousness arises from conditions, [one realizes its empty nature].
How could one calculate that there is a deity who causes one to know or mistakenly grasp?
When the eye-faculty encounters the object-field of form,
visual consciousness arises immediately.
When visual consciousness arises,
it cognizes the object-field of form; therefore,
it is called the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).
Second, the auditory consciousness element (*śrotravijñānadhātu*): when the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*) encounters the object of sound (*śabdaviṣaya*), auditory consciousness arises.
At the moment auditory consciousness arises, [it is the auditory consciousness element].
It is the consciousness that cognizes the object-field of sound; therefore, it is called the auditory consciousness element (*śrotravijñānadhātu*).
Third, the olfactory consciousness element (*ghrāṇavijñānadhātu*): when the olfactory faculty encounters the object-field of odor...
Thereupon, olfactory consciousness arises.
When olfactory consciousness arises,
it immediately cognizes the object-field of fragrance.
Therefore, it is called the nose-consciousness element (ghrāṇavijñānadhātu).
Fourth, the tongue-consciousness element (jihvāvijñānadhātu): when the tongue faculty encounters the object of taste, tongue-consciousness arises.
When gustatory consciousness arises,
it cognizes the object of taste; therefore,
it is called the gustatory consciousness element (*jihvāvijñānadhātu*).
Regarding the fifth, the body-consciousness element: when the body faculty encounters the object of tangibles, body-consciousness arises.
At the time that body-consciousness arises,
It is precisely the consciousness that cognizes the object of touch;
therefore, it is called the element of body-consciousness.
Sixth, the element of mental consciousness: once the five consciousnesses have arisen, they immediately cease.
The mind is the mental consciousness.
This mental consciousness arises in succession.
When the mental consciousness arises, it...
It is precisely the consciousness of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*). If the five consciousnesses can give rise to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
then the preceding five consciousnesses serve as its faculty (*indriya*).
The subsequent mental consciousness acts as the mental consciousness.
When this mental consciousness ceases, the succeeding consciousness arises in its place;
thus, the preceding mental consciousness gives rise to the subsequent mental consciousness.
In this way, one also departs from the conventional designations of "root" (*indriya*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*);
rather, that which is capable of producing is designated as the root,
and that which is produced is designated as consciousness.
Now, the consciousness that arises is explained as the *manovijñānadhātu* (the sphere of mental consciousness).

**Chapter Five: The First Gate of the Sixteen Views** 1. Self (*ātman*) 2. Sentient being (*sattva*) 3. Life-principle (*jīva*) 4. Living being (*poṣa*) 5. One who is born (*jantu*) 6. One who is nourished (*puruṣa*) 7. A person (*pudgala*) 8. An agent (*kāraka*) 9. One who causes to act (*hetukāraka*) 10. One who arises (*utthāpaka*) 11. One who causes to arise (*samutthāpaka*) 12. One who experiences (*vedaka*) 13. One who causes to experience (*samvedaka*) 14. One who knows (*jñātṛ*) 15. One who sees (*paśyaka*) Next, [follow] name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*).
As for distinguishing the sixteen types of views:
within phenomena such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
a self (*ātman*) is fundamentally unfindable.
Those who have not yet seen the Path all falsely imagine a self within phenomena such as name-and-form.
Regarding "what belongs to me" (*mamakāra*): an analysis of the mind that conceives of a self,
categorized according to its various conditions.
There are thus sixteen distinct types of views and cognitions;
when extensively applied to various conditions,
false conceptualizations become beyond counting.
Because of these inversions, all afflictions,
the cycle of birth and death, and karmic activities arise in full. Now,
for the purpose of clarifying later on all gates of contemplation, such as the two kinds of emptiness regarding persons and phenomena, and so forth:
One must properly discern the nature of phenomena as being either provisional or real;
therefore, I shall briefly explain this based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. First, regarding the self (*ātman*):
if one lacks clear understanding due to ignorance concerning the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*).
Whether in identity or in difference,
one falsely conceives of a real self and what belongs to a self;
therefore, it is called "ātman" (self).

Second, regarding sentient beings (*sattva*): within the composite of dharmas such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*), they falsely conceptualize the existence of a self;
therefore, they are called "sentient beings."

Third, the "life-sustainer" (jīvaka): within the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements, one falsely conceives of a self that experiences the life-span of karmic fruition, which may be long or short;
therefore, it is called the "life-sustainer."

The "living being" (jīva): within the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements, one falsely conceives of a self as a life-faculty that is established, continuous, and uninterrupted;
therefore, it is called a "living being."
Regarding the five types of birth: within the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements,
one falsely conceives of a "self" that initiates various activities,
just as a father gives birth to a son.
One who is called "a being born" (jāta) is so named because they conceive of themselves as having come to receive birth among human beings; therefore,
they are called "a being born."
Sixth, nourishing: within the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, bases, and elements, one falsely conceives that "I" can nourish others;
therefore, it is called nourishing.
Furthermore, one reckons that from birth until now,
one has been nurtured by one's parents;
therefore, it is called "nurturing."
The seven categories of beings: within the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*),
they falsely imagine that there is a self possessing these five aggregates,
twelve bases, eighteen elements, and other such causal conditions.
Because these various phenomena (*dharma*) possess numerical categories, they are called "numerical aggregates" (*saṃkhyā*).

Regarding the eight types of persons: within the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), one falsely conceives of a self as being "the practitioner."
Because he differs from those who do not practice,
he is called a "human"; furthermore,
he conceives that he has been born into the human realm.
Because they differ from other paths, they are called "human beings. Regarding the nine types of agents:
within the phenomena of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) of name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
One falsely imagines that the self possesses a body, strength, hands, and feet,
and is capable of performing actions;
therefore, it is called the "agent."
The "maker of the proclivities" refers to one who, within the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, the sense bases, and the elements,
falsely conceives of a self that can employ others; therefore,
it is called the maker of the proclivities.

Regarding "the one who arises" (utthāpaka): within the phenomena of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the aggregates (skandha), the sense-bases (āyatana), and the elements (dhātu), one falsely conceives of a self that can create the karma of future merit and demerit;
therefore, it is called "the one who arises."

Regarding the "ariser of the twelve latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*): within the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, bases, and elements, one falsely conceives of a self that can cause others to give rise to karma of future merit or demerit;
therefore, it is called the "ariser of the latent tendencies."

Thirteenth, the experiencer (*vedaka*): within the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), one falsely imagines that "I" shall experience the retribution of merit and demerit in a future body;
therefore, it is called the experiencer.
The "one who causes others to experience" (sārthavāha) refers to one who, among the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, bases, and elements,
falsely conceives of a self that shall cause others to experience the retributive fruits of suffering and happiness; therefore,
they are called "the one who causes others to experience."
Fifteenth, the "knower" (jñātṛ): among the phenomena of name-and-form, the aggregates, bases, and elements, one falsely imagines that there are five faculties capable of knowing the five objects;
therefore, it is called the "knower."
Regarding the sixteen views: within the phenomena of the aggregates, bases, and elements such as name-and-form,
one falsely conceives that because I possess the eye faculty,
I am able to see all forms.
Furthermore, one conceives that "I am able to give rise to wrong views," and that "I who give rise to right views" am the "seer. Chapter Six:
The Initial Gate of the Two Afflictions of Views and Craving. 1. The Affliction of Views. 2. The Affliction of Craving. Next, regarding the aggregates, bases, and elements (*skandha-āyatana-dhātu*):
Including ourselves, there are sixteen [kinds of views].
As for those who distinguish between views and craving:
if one is deluded regarding these two types of phenomena—the provisional and the real—[one falls into error].
Consequently, inverted perceptions arise in profusion; thus,
the cycle of transmigration through the three realms is boundless,
all brought about by the influence of afflictions.
If one discusses the root of afflictions,
they do not go beyond views and craving;
their branches and twigs are merely conceptual distinctions.
Thus, the categories are very numerous:
namely, the three poisons, the five hindrances, the ten fetters,
and the ninety-eight afflictions.
Whether numbering eighty-four thousand, or even as many as the sands of the Ganges,
although these categories differ in their numerical extent,
they are all equally the power of afflictions that moisten and sustain rebirth.
In essence, there is no distinction;
it is merely that the skillful means of the teaching establish these categories based on the varying numbers of factors.
Therefore, the *Sutra of the Necklace* (*Sengluo jing*) states:
"Seeing and attachment— these two dharmas— delude the form and mind of the dharma-realm,
giving rise extensively to all the afflictions of the triple world."
Regarding the general name "affliction" (*kleśa*):
"affliction" (*fan*) takes the sense of clamor and vexation as its meaning;
"distress" (*nao*) takes the sense of oppression and disorder as its meaning.
The dharmas capable of clamoring and vexing force the practitioner’s mind and spirit into turmoil,
thereby preventing true illumination from being developed;
for this reason, they are called *kleśa* (afflictions).
The first is the affliction of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). To contemplate reality with a distorted mind is called "view.
If, regarding the principles of the provisional and the real, one is deluded in sentiment and erroneously seeks through inverted conceptions, it is so named.
To falsely cling to a partial principle as being real according to one's views is collectively termed "view.
Regarding the afflictions of view:
This refers to the five sharp fetters (*pañca tīkṣṇānuśayāḥ*),
the eighty-eight fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*),
and the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭayaḥ*), and so forth.
Second, the affliction of craving: a mind stained by greed is called craving.
Whether toward conventional or ultimate phenomena, one’s emotions become deluded and follow the dictates of the mind.
Attachment and entanglement toward all objects and circumstances encountered are collectively termed "craving" (tṛṣṇā).
The afflictions of attachment refer to the five dull underlying tendencies (*mūla-anuśaya*) and the ten underlying tendencies abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

And the outflows (*āsrava*) of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are to be abandoned—namely, the yokes (*yoga*), the graspings (*grantha*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

**Chapter Seven: The Initial Gate of the Three Poisons.** 1. The poison of greed (*rāga-viṣa*). 2. The poison of hatred (*dveṣa-viṣa*). 3. The poison of delusion (*moha-viṣa*). Next, the three poisons are distinguished following the [discussion of] views and craving.
Since these two categories differ in being either combined or separate,
they must be distinguished.
If they were combined, one would take only a single portion of delusion (*moha*) as view (*dṛṣṭi*).
The remaining portion, along with greed and anger,
are combined to form craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
If they are separated, each of these— viewing, craving, and so forth— contains the three poisons within it.
Thus, by traversing the three realms and five destinies,
one departs from the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
All afflictions are collectively termed "poisons."
"Poison" (du) takes "deep-seated toxicity" as its meaning.
Because it is extremely destructive and corrupting,
it is called "deep-seated poison."
Because it can destroy supramundane wholesome states of mind, it is called "poison.
First, the poison of greed: the mind that draws things toward itself is termed greed.
If one uses a deluded mind to confront all objects that accord with one's desires and seeks them out without satiety,
this is the poison of greed.
Throughout the three realms and five elements,
the fifteen latent tendencies of greed are all forms of the poison of greed;
however, because the afflictions in the two upper realms are already thin, [they do not manifest].
It receives the name "craving" (tṛṣṇā) because it is distinct [from other afflictions]. Second, as for the poison of hatred (dveṣa):
that which opposes and provokes anger is called hatred.
If, with a deluded mind, one encounters any object contrary to one's feelings and immediately gives rise to anger,
this is the poison of hatred.
Descending from the five categories of the desire realm,
there are immediately the five latent tendencies of anger;
these are all the poisons of hatred.
According to the interpretation of several masters, there is no hatred (*dveṣa*) in the two upper realms.
Regarding the three poisons of delusion (*moha*): the mind that is confused is called delusion.
If one is confused regarding all phenomena of fact and principle, it is delusion.
Due to ignorance and lack of understanding,
one is deluded and falsely grasps,
giving rise to various erroneous practices.
This is precisely the poison of delusion,
also called ignorance (*avidyā*).
There are two kinds of ignorance.
The first is associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*),
which arises in conjunction with the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms and five aggregates.

The second is dissociated ignorance (*viprayukta-avidyā*), which refers to the fifteen latent tendencies of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*) within the three realms and five aggregates. **Chapter Eight: The First Gate of the Five Hindrances** 1.

The hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*). 2. The hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*). 3. The hindrance of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*). 4. The hindrance of restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*). 5. The hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*). Regarding the explanation of the five hindrances following the three poisons (*triviṣa*): [text continues]
If one discusses the essence of the three poisons,
how could they differ from the five hindrances?
It is merely that their categories and headings are different.
There are differences regarding the increase and decrease of names;
therefore, they are distinguished next.
The reason for this is as follows:
If one eliminates the designation "poison of delusion" and remains free from the phenomena of delusion,
yet possesses the three hindrances of sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt,
together with greed and hatred, these constitute the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*).
If one opens the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), afflictions (*kleśa*) become immeasurable.
They are collectively termed "hindrances" because their meaning is that of covering and obscuring.
They are called "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa) because they can cover the practitioner's pure and wholesome mind, preventing it from being developed.

Since these five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*) are clearly identified as the primary obstacles to the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) explained below, their characteristics must be briefly distinguished.
First, the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*): the insatiable grasping of the mind constitutes sensual desire.
The analysis of its essential nature and characteristics is fully explained as in the section on the poison of greed.
Among the fifteen latent tendencies of greed within the three realms and five modes of activity:
These are the hindrance of sensual desire and the second, the hindrance of ill will. A mind of anger is called ill will;
this is its definition and characteristic.
It is as previously explained.
The five modes and five types of latent tendencies of anger (*pratighānuśaya*) in the desire realm are precisely the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpādāvaraṇa*).
Third, the hindrance of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*): the dulling and maturing of the mental consciousness is called "sloth" (*styāna*);
the obscuration and darkness of the five sensory faculties is termed "torpor" (*middha*).
If the mind relies upon the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then ignorance (*avidyā*) increases.
When the mental consciousness becomes drowsy and matures [into sleep],
and the five sense-faculties are darkened and obscured such that nothing is perceived,
this is called "sleep."
Some authorities state that these are increased mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
They are nonetheless subsumed under the fifteen delusions (*moha-anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-heya*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the four hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of restlessness and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*): the movement of thoughts with a deviant mind is called restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Reflecting on this with regret, one becomes weary and distressed.
If one indulges in ignorance and grasps erroneously,
then the mind will become agitated by frivolous conceptual proliferation.
Since one's actions have gone astray,
there will be anxiety and regret upon reflection; this,
too, is an increase in the mental factors (caitta-dharma).
It precisely comprises the thirty-two views and proclivities (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*);
it also includes a small portion of those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The five hindrances of doubt: when the deluded mind seeks the principle yet wavers and fails to reach a decision,
it is called doubt.
If one cultivates dharmas such as meditative concentration (samādhi) on the path of cultivation,
yet remains obscured by the dullness of ignorance (avidyā),
one will fail to distinguish between the true and the false.
To give rise to hesitation and for the mind to lack decisive resolution—
these are all termed doubt.
The doubts common in the world are not the one true treatise;
they are doubts that obstruct the Path.

These are the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*): namely, the twelve latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) consisting of four modes within each of the three realms.

**Chapter Nine: The First Gate of the Ten Latent Tendencies** The five dull latent tendencies (*pañca-mṛdu-anuśaya*): 1. The latent tendency of greed (*rāga*). 2. The latent tendency of hatred (*pratigha*). 3. The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā*). 4. The latent tendency of pride (*māna*). 5. The latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā*). The five sharp latent tendencies (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*): 1. The latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). 2. The latent tendency of the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). 3. The latent tendency of false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*). 4. The latent tendency of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). 5. The latent tendency of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Next, following the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), the ten latent tendencies are explained.
How could the ten fetters (daśa-saṃyojana) be different from the five hindrances (pañca-nīvaraṇa)?
If the teaching is intended solely for those practicing meditative concentration (samādhi),
it establishes the number of the three poisons (tri-viṣa) and the five hindrances in an abbreviated manner.
If it is explained for those cultivating wisdom,
in order to ensure that they clearly recognize the delusions to be abandoned without error,
it is necessary to distinguish them as the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The reason for this is that the two hindrances of greed and hatred are themselves the two underlying tendencies of greed and hatred.
The root of the hindrance of sloth and torpor is the latent tendency of delusion;
by departing from delusion, one transcends conceit.
These constitute the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*). The hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) is the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
These are the five dull latent tendencies (*pañca-mṛdu-anuśayāḥ*).
Restlessness and regret are precisely a mind that is agitated by improper reflection.
If their characteristics are analyzed in detail,
there is a distinction between five types of sharp and five types of dull underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
If one traces this back, it is still the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*);
when analyzed, they become the ten underlying tendencies (*daśānuśaya*). If one further expands upon these ten underlying tendencies...
Thus they give rise to all afflictions.
These ten are collectively termed "messengers" (*paryavasthāna*).
"Messenger" takes the sense of driving and employing [others].
Because they are able to drive and enslave the mind and spirit of the practitioner,
causing them to transmigrate through the three realms, they are collectively given the name "fetter" (*saṃyojana*).
They are also called the ten afflictions (*kleśa*).
The meaning of "affliction" is as previously explained.
First is the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-anuśaya*), which is insatiable seeking and grasping.
It is called craving.
To analyze its characteristics is as fully explained in the section on the poison of craving.
Those abandoned through the vision and cultivation [of the truths]—
the fifteen types of greed within the five categories across the three realms—
are all the latent tendency of greed.
Second is the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*);
the state of mind characterized by anger is called "aversion.
Its specific characteristics are now to be analyzed.
This is as explained in the section on the poison of hatred (*dveṣa-viṣa*).
It is abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation;
among the five types of conduct in the desire realm, it corresponds to the five forms of ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
This is precisely the latent tendency of ill-will (*pratighānuśaya*).
Third, the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*): the deluded mind that lacks clear understanding is called ignorance.
If one perceives objects with a deluded mind,
then whatever arises will be lost forever, moment by moment.
Those who do not know shame or remorse are all deluded;
this is severed by the vision of the truths and by cultivation.
The fifteen types of delusion (*moha*) within the three realms and five modes of activity are the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*).
Regarding the four latent tendencies of pride (*māna-anuśaya*): pride is defined as the mind that esteems oneself and looks down upon others.
If one, relying on one's own lineage, wealth, status, virtue, or talent,
treats others with contempt,
this is pride (*māna*).
There are eight types of pride,
which will be detailed below;
they extend to those abandoned through the elimination of views and afflictions.
The fifteen types of pride (*māna*) within the three realms and five destinies are all the latent tendencies of pride (*mānānuśaya*).
The five latent tendencies of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*) cause the mind to be deluded and to deviate from principle.
To be hesitant and unable to reach a decision is called doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Its characteristics are distinguished in detail,
as explained in the section on the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*).
The twelve kinds of doubt regarding the three realms and four modes of conduct are all the latent tendencies of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).

As for the six latent tendencies of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*): if, within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)...
To falsely conceptualize [the aggregates] as a self is called the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
This occurs when one fails to understand due to ignorance.
Thus, within the five aggregates,
twenty kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi arise; therefore,
there are twenty types of satkāyadṛṣṭi.
Those abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*). Within one category [of views], there are two types of self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) spanning the three realms.
There are seven latent tendencies of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi-anuśaya*), which are the minds that cling to extremes.
This is called the view of extremes.
It refers to failing to understand the four extremes and instead adhering to them through one's views.
One side is true, while all other sides are false,
according to what has been seen.
Each adhering to one extreme,
they all fall into views of partiality,
traversing the five aggregates throughout the three periods of time.
There are thus sixty-two views;
all of these are abandoned by the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya).
Taken together, they constitute the sixty-two views.
These are likewise subsumed under one-sided views (*ekāntadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, with respect to what is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*),
there are three types of one-sided views within a single mode of activity as it traverses the three realms.
The eighth is the underlying tendency of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*). It is called "wrong view" because it grasps principles with a distorted mind.
If there is ignorance (*avidyā*), one does not clearly understand the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths.
With a perverse mind,
they reject and deny this principle,
thereby severing their supramundane roots of goodness.
Even to the point of practicing the conduct of an icchantika regarding worldly roots of goodness— this is false view.
Among the four modes of the three realms that are abandoned through the vision of the truths,
there are twelve types of wrong views;
these are the nine fetters of dogmatic attachment to views, which [arise] regarding things that are not truly superior.
One erroneously perceives nirvana and gives rise to a mind that grasps it; therefore,
it is called "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
When practicing the Way, although one may enter various gates of contemplation,
true illumination has not yet arisen.
Due to ignorance and lack of clear understanding,
one erroneously calculates what has been obtained,
regarding it as real and as supreme.
To give rise to a mind of attachment is all termed "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa); it is abandoned through the realization of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya).
Regarding the three realms and four modes of activity,
there are twelve types of views that constitute the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
There are ten types of the proclivity of grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-anuśaya*), which pertain to what is not true morality.
One erroneously regards these as precepts and adopts them for practice; therefore,
it is called "clinging to precepts" (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
If one takes the precepts of chickens, dogs,
or oxen, or even the precepts practiced by the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders,
and regards them as true precepts.
All these are termed "clinging to precepts.
Even if a person upholds the Buddha's precepts,
they perceive the characteristics of those precepts.

This is also the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). It is comprised of two modes within the three realms and is severed by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*);
there are six types of such clinging to precepts and observances.

10. The First Gate of the Ninety-eight Proclivities (Anuśaya): The Tenth Gate of the Truths (Dṛṣṭi). There are eighty-eight proclivities. Within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu), there are thirty-two proclivities; within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are twenty-eight proclivities; and within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there are twenty-eight proclivities. Regarding the Gate of Contemplation (Bhāvanā), there are ten proclivities: four in the realm of desire, three in the realm of form, and three in the formless realm. Following these ten proclivities, the ninety-eight proclivities are thus distinguished.
This is precisely because the obstacles of delusion differ between the two paths of seeing and cultivation;
it is intended to enable those practicing contemplation to clearly recognize the specific delusions to be remedied.
To ensure that the abandonment and suppression [of defilements] are not confused, the teaching proceeds through the three realms and five modes of activity,
making detailed distinctions among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Thus, there are ninety-eight;
they are also called the ninety-eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
Collectively, they are termed *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).
Regarding what is called "affliction" (*kleśa*),
its classification is as explained previously.
If one is free from the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Thus, all afflictions are eliminated.
Now, according to the followers of the *Saṃkhyā* school, we shall clarify the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
As for the followers of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*:
The interpretations differ.

Regarding the delusions of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are thirty-two underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): ten underlying tendencies are present under the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), and seven underlying tendencies are present under the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).

Excluding the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and the clinging to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), there are seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) beneath the truth of cessation (nirodhasatya);
these likewise exclude the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and the clinging to rules and rituals.
Beneath the Truth of the Path, there are eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
excluding only the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, beneath the four modes of conduct in the desire realm...
In total, there are thirty-two *anuśayas*.

Regarding the delusions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*), there are twenty-eight *anuśayas*: under the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there are nine *anuśayas*, excluding hatred (*pratigha*);
under the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), there are six *anuśayas*, excluding hatred.

Furthermore, excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Under the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*), there are six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
these likewise exclude anger (*vyāpāda*), the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and attachment to precepts and rituals.
Below the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya), there are seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya);
these also exclude the underlying tendency of aversion (pratigha) as well as the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
Therefore, below the four aspects of the form realm (rūpadhātu)...
In total, there are twenty-eight *anuśayas*.

Regarding the delusions of the truths to be seen (*satyadarśana-heya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are twenty-eight *anuśayas*: nine *anuśayas* under the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and six *anuśayas* under the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
Beneath the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya) there are six underlying tendencies (anuśaya); beneath the truth of the path (mārga-satya) there are seven underlying tendencies.
Whether they are grasped or eliminated.
All are as analyzed in the section on the Form Realm;
therefore, the four modes of activity in the Formless Realm, when combined with the twenty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), total thirty-two.
Within the four truths of the three realms,
there are eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*);
these are all afflictions that obstruct the vision of the truths.
These are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) by those who have attained the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
A brief explanation of the characteristics of these proclivities (*anuśaya*) is provided here;
they are all as analyzed in the previous chapter on the ten categories of proclivities.
Contemplating the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm: first, the underlying tendency of greed;
second, the underlying tendency of hatred; third, the underlying tendency of delusion.
The four latent tendencies of pride:
these tendencies are abandoned through the path of cultivation upon entering the stage of the candidate for the fruit of once-returning.
Up to the fruit of Anāgāmin, the nine grades [of afflictions] are finally exhausted.
Regarding the objects of contemplation, there are three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the form realm: first, the underlying tendency of attachment (*rāga*).
The second is the latent tendency of delusion; the third is the latent tendency of pride.
These three latent tendencies are all present in those who are candidates for arhatship.
One abandons them by means of the path of cultivation and wisdom.
Regarding the delusions of the formless realm, there are three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): first, the underlying tendency of greed;
second, the underlying tendency of delusion.
There are three types of pride-fetters (*māna-anuśaya*).

Thus, the afflictions of the realm of thought (*bhavāgra*) in the three realms comprise ten fetters in total; when added to the previously mentioned view-afflictions (*darśana-heya*), [the total is sixteen].
Together, these constitute ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).
However, these three proclivities are also abandoned during the stage of the candidate for Arhatship (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*),
and are only completely exhausted upon reaching the fruit.
Next, one should extensively set forth the categories of the various afflictions (*kleśa*),
namely: the three outflows (*āsrava*) and the four currents (*ogha*).
The four bonds,
the eight perversions,
and the eight inversions.
The nine fetters,
the nine afflictions,
and the ten envelopments.
Up to five hundred afflictions,
eighty-four thousand gateways of defilement,
and afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All [these fetters] are distinguished through the combination and separation of the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of view and craving;
if one were to set forth their categories in full, it would be as follows... [and so on].

Now, I shall briefly set forth several categories sufficient to clarify the gate of teaching regarding the methods by which afflictions combine and separate, and how delusions and hindrances moisten the process of rebirth.
These are the various headings for the afflictions.
In the sixth fascicle, this will be further elaborated upon according to the essentials.

11. The First Gate of the Ten Evil Deeds, Part Eleven. There are three evils of the body: first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct. There are four evils of speech: first, false speech; second, divisive speech; third, harsh speech; fourth, frivolous speech. There are three evils of the mind: first, covetousness; second, malice; third, wrong views. These ten evils are distinguished next after the various afflictions (*kleśa*) and fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Since afflictions are by nature delusive phenomena,
they are able to drive and enslave the practitioner’s mind and spirit,
causing them to perceive objects in a distorted manner.
If one indulges these deluded emotions and gives rise to actions of body, speech, and mind,
then one's movements will deviate from the principle;
therefore, regarding that which arises from the three karmas:
These constitute the ten evils. As for their general designation as "evil" (akuśala),
"evil" takes the meaning of being contrary to principle.
These ten all arise in contravention of reason;
therefore, they are called "evil" and are also termed the "ten unwholesome paths."
Because it leads to the retribution of suffering, it is not a wholesome path.
First, killing: to sever the lives of all sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called "killing.
Second is stealing: taking another's property.
Therefore, it is called "stealing."
Third, sexual misconduct: engaging in sexual acts with those who are not one's wife or consort;
therefore, it is called sexual misconduct.
Fourth, false speech: deceiving others with one's words.
Therefore, it is called false speech.
Fifth, double-tongued speech: using words that incite strife to create divisions between others, causing them to experience gain or loss.
To be divisive is called double-tongued speech.
Sixth is harsh speech: to address others with abusive words so as to cause them distress.
The seventh is frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). Frivolous speech refers to words and expressions that deviate from reason;
it is called frivolous speech.
Eighth, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*): to draw in objects of the senses that accord with one's inclinations,
with a mind that knows no satiety,
is called sensual desire.
Ninth, ill will (*vyāpāda*): when the mind gives rise to anger in response to an adverse object,
it is called ill will.
The ten wrong views: to deny the cause and effect of the correct [Dharma],
or to seek blessings through perverse faith—
both are termed wrong views.
Next, one should expound upon the four grave offenses,
the five heinous crimes,
and the seven heinous crimes.
They slander the Vaipulya sutras,
misappropriate the property of the Sangha,
and engage in the conduct of icchantikas.
The sixteen types of improper discipline (*akuśala-vinaya*) and other categories of light and heavy evil karma all originate from within the ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala*).
Regarding the explanation made through the analysis of separation and combination:
I now wish to discuss the essential gateways for entering the various paths,
as fully set forth in the text, up to the sixth fascicle.

It shall be explained further elsewhere. **Chapter Twelve: The First Gate of the Ten Wholesome Actions** The three kinds of wholesome conduct of the body: 1. Refraining from killing; 2. Refraining from stealing; 3. Refraining from sexual misconduct. The four kinds of wholesome conduct of speech: 1. Refraining from false speech; 2. Refraining from divisive speech; 3. Refraining from harsh speech; 4. Refraining from frivolous speech. The three kinds of wholesome conduct of the mind: 1. Refraining from covetousness; 2. Refraining from ill-will; 3. Refraining from wrong views. Regarding the explanation of the ten wholesome actions following the ten unwholesome actions: [the wholesome are established as the opposites of the unwholesome].
If a person can understand that evil is conduct contrary to principle,
and thus brings about suffering in both the present and the future,
they must necessarily cease evil and practice goodness.
This can lead to the eternal attainment of the fruit of pure transcendence in future lives;
for this reason, the ten wholesome actions are explained immediately following the ten unwholesome actions.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of the ten wholesome actions.
First, cessation;
second, practice.
Cessation means simply stopping prior unwholesome states.
Not causing affliction to others,
one practices superior virtues when acting,
bringing benefit and peace to all.
These two are collectively termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
"Wholesome" takes the meaning of being in accord with principle;
it brings the cessation of inversions and the return to the truth.
Therefore, it is said that they accord with principle:
through cessation, one rests from the evils of profound delusion;
through practice, one gradually returns to the goodness of the supreme path.
Therefore, both cessation and cultivation are termed "wholesome," or they may be further designated by the name "the Path."
This is because it enables one to reach the fruit of ultimate bliss.
First, abstaining from taking life is the "virtue of restraint";
it restrains the unwholesome conduct of killing that preceded it.
The virtuous person should practice the virtue of releasing living beings.
Second is non-stealing, which is a wholesome restraint;
it stops the unwholesome conduct of stealing the wealth and property of others.
The virtuous should practice the virtue of giving.
Third is non-licentiousness, which is the virtue of restraint;
it involves ceasing the unwholesome conduct of sexual desire for those who are not one's wife or consort.
The virtuous should practice the virtue of reverence.
The four types of non-false speech constitute the virtue of restraint;
they restrain the unwholesome conduct of uttering empty words to deceive others.
The virtuous should practice the virtue of truthful speech.
The five forms of non-slanderous speech constitute the virtue of restraint;
they restrain the evil conduct of inciting conflict between two parties.
The virtuous should practice the virtue of harmony.
The six types of non-malicious speech constitute the virtue of restraint;
they restrain the previous evil words and the harmful actions directed toward others.
The virtuous should practice the virtue of gentle speech.
The seven forms of non-frivolous speech constitute the virtue of restraint;
they involve ceasing the unwholesome practice of frivolous speech that is biased, perverse, and contrary to reason.
The virtuous should practice meaningful speech that brings benefit; this is the excellence of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kuśala*).
The eight forms of non-covetousness are the excellence of restraint (*saṃvara-kuśala*), which stops the previously mentioned unwholesome conduct of insatiable grasping.
Those who are virtuous should practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
To contemplate all six sense objects as deceptive and impure is the practice of the virtue of meditation (*samādhi-kuśala*).
Ninth, non-anger is the virtue of tranquility (*śamatha-kuśala*).
Cease the evil conduct of prior anger;
the virtuous should practice the goodness of loving-kindness and patience.
The ten non-erroneous views are themselves the cessation of evil.
Cease the evil conduct of rejecting the correct [teachings on] cause and effect and harboring perverse faith and deviant thoughts.
Those who are good should practice right faith, turn their hearts toward the True Path, and give rise to the wholesome mind of wisdom.
The First Gate of the Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm, Volume One, Part One of the First Section.
